extracted.intended_audience: researchers and science communicators (clinical trialists, journal editors, press officers)
extracted.subtask_short: identifying spin in RCTs and PRs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for detecting and classifying 'spin' in randomized controlled trial (RCT) reports, abstracts, and associated press releases; includes categories, levels, prevalence, and factors associated with misleading interpretations. Useful for evaluating scientific articles and their press communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'spin'
rubrics_metrics.description: “Spin” as a way of reporting to convince the reader that the beneficial effect (efficacy, safety) of the experimental treatment is higher than shown by the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this working definition when evaluating text for deliberate or inadvertent over-optimistic presentation. Look for wording that enhances perceived benefit beyond the actual data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: In RCTs, data should speak for themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: In RCTs, data should speak for themselves; scientists and sponsors are rarely neutral regarding the results of their trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising reports, be aware of motives that introduce bias: delay and level of publication, promotion of use in clinical practice, future career or profit. Recognize that broad latitude in writing an article can bias presentation and interpretation of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of spin by article section
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether 'spin' appears in specific sections: Title, Results, Discussion, Conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure prevalence by section (slide shows prevalence across Title, Results, Discussion, Conclusion). >40% of reports had 'spin' in at least 2 of the 3 sections of the main text. Use section-level checks when coding articles for spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Claim of equivalence or comparable effectiveness (conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim of equivalence or comparable effectiveness in the conclusion despite negative or non-significant primary outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example wording to flag: phrasing that asserts comparable effect without appropriate statistical support. This was observed in the sample (6/72; 8%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Particular focus on statistically significant results (conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular focus on statistically significant (often secondary) results while downplaying nonsignificant primary outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot emphasis on significant secondary analyses or subgroup findings as the main take-away; observed in study (8/72; 11%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Linguistic 'spin' only (conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of language that suggests benefit or positive interpretation without substantive statistical support (purely linguistic spin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for optimistic phrasing (e.g., 'is expected to be a very important modality') or euphemisms for non-significance (e.g., 'approached, but did not achieve conventional statistical significance'). Observed (5/72; 7%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Ruling out an adverse event (conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusive statements excluding harm (adverse events) despite insufficient evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: definitive claims that an adverse event is 'unaltered' or 'not increased' when study lacks power or evidence to make such claims. Observed (22/72; 31%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Focusing on overall group assessment (conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting that emphasizes overall group-level improvements in both groups to obscure lack of between-group difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrasing that highlights clinical relevance within groups rather than acknowledging no difference between treatments. Observed (9/72; 13%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Recommendation to use the treatment (conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concluding recommendation to use or adopt the experimental treatment despite negative primary outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag any conclusion that recommends clinical use when the primary outcome was non-significant. Observed (3/72; 4%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Focus on another objective (conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifting the narrative to a different objective or outcome (reporting as if not a comparative RCT) to avoid addressing the negative primary result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for emphasis on secondary endpoints or ancillary analyses framed as primary findings. Observed (3/72; 4%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Other misleading conclusion types
rubrics_metrics.description: Other forms of misleading interpretation, e.g., claiming both treatments superior to a historical placebo control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catch unusual or inferential leaps that are not supported by the trial design or data (observed 4/72; 6%). Provide concrete counterexamples when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of spin (no/low/moderate/high)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify the overall level of spin in an article/abstract/press release as no spin, low level, moderate level, or high level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High level of 'spin' defined by absence of acknowledgement of the negative primary outcome, no expressed uncertainty, and no recommendation for further trials. Use this ordinal scale to grade severity; slides show distribution for abstract and article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congruence between abstract conclusion and press release (spin relationship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify the relationship between spin in the published abstract conclusion and the press release (e.g., no spin in both; spin added in PR; spin deleted in PR; same spin in both; same spin plus new spin in PR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this mapping to detect amplification or mitigation of spin when results move from abstract to press release. Factors associated with spin in PR include presence of spin in the abstract conclusion (RR = 3.8 [1.5-9.3]) and, in multivariate analysis, sample size, impact factor, journal, and primary outcome result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation polarity (article and press release)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize the interpretation of results as 'In favor', 'Neutral', or 'Not in favor' of the experimental treatment for both the article and the press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare polarity across article and PR (slides show 79% of articles 'In favor' vs 58% for PRs, etc.). Use this coding to quantify tendency toward favorable interpretation in different media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadequate interpretation from press releases (over- vs under-estimation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether press releases provide an inadequate interpretation by overestimating or underestimating the treatment's beneficial effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the sample, 22/71 press releases (31%) had inadequate interpretation: 19/22 (86%) overestimated beneficial effect, 3/22 (14%) underestimated. Flag PRs that exaggerate effect sizes, causal claims, or omit key non-significant primary outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors associated with overestimation in PRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Contextual factors that increase likelihood of overestimation of benefit in press releases: specialist journal, negative primary outcome, small sample size (<110), and presence of spin in the press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slides present comparisons and p-values (e.g., for specialist journal: 45% overestimation when spin present vs 6% when no spin, p=0.002). Use these factors as predictors when auditing PRs for likely overstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definition of 'negative RCT' for spin studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a 'negative RCT' as a randomized controlled trial with primary outcome p≥0.05 when identifying spin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sampling studies to assess spin prevalence, restrict to trials with non-significant primary outcomes (p≥0.05) to examine how authors/press releases interpret null results. This was the sampling criterion used (N=72).
